entries.title: Senate Democrats Want a New Leader, but Nobody Wants to Do the Job
entries.summary: Only Sen. Chris Van Hollen has expressed any interest in challenging longtime leader Chuck Schumer. Schumer insists he’s on track to win the top spot.
entries.content:
Plenty of Senate Democratic caucus members are lukewarm about backing Chuck Schumer for majority leader. But nobody is stepping forward to challenge him.

After a closed-door Senate Democratic Caucus meeting on Tuesday, Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Bernie Sanders held a news conference to push for new blood in leadership. Michigan’s Slotkin said the team should govern for “folks from blue states, purple states and red states.” But both also said they weren’t interested in running.

“I am not actively seeking this job,” Slotkin said. “I am seeking change.”

While many have seen the midterm election results as a backlash against President Donald Trump and Republicans, the pair framed it as a call for a shake-up in the Democratic Party as well.

Slotkin said she could vote for Schumer but that she first wanted to see “a plan on how they’re going to govern differently, what they’re going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people’s pockets and then in particular how they’re going to communicate differently.”

“I like Chuck,” Vermont’s independent Sen. Sanders said. “But in my view the time is now for change.”

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is the only Democrat who’s indicated any interest, but neither senator endorsed him. Slotkin said they had a “productive conversation” yesterday.

Van Hollen said he was “listening” to the calls for change and calling his Senate colleagues.

“We just saw democracy in America in action, we should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate and a little more democracy to the United States Senate Democratic Caucus,” Van Hollen said at a Tuesday event hosted by the progressive group Groundwork Action.

Minutes later, at his own news conference just a floor below Sanders and Slotkin’s, Schumer shrugged off any possible challenge, saying, “We have great unity in our caucus,” and that he is “confident” he will be elected. The consummate insider has served in Washington for more than four decades and spent nearly a decade leading the Senate Democratic Caucus.

Some of the Democrats elected from red states who worked to distance themselves from the national Democratic brand previously said they would not support Schumer. They include Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina. Hamilton and Andrews have both declined to support Schumer in TV interviews since the election. Prior to Tuesday’s meeting, Sen. Raphael Warnock told CNN he wasn’t ready to support any candidate before hearing their case.

Sen.-elect Troy Jackson of Maine reiterated his anti-Schumer stance to The Washington Sun on Monday but didn’t suggest an alternative candidate.

“Don’t know,” Jackson said when asked who he’d back instead. “Haven’t been asked.”

Most Senate Democrats, however, are closing ranks around Schumer after the party’s unexpectedly good results in the midterms. Democrats flipped seven seats, and two other Republican incumbents are trailing in their races in Alaska and Mississippi.

Chuck Schumer (5300x3533, AR: 1.50)
“This caucus is grateful for the hard work of Senator Schumer,” Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York practically yelled as she emphatically tapped the lectern at Schumer’s news conference. “And that is why you will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position.”

“What have these two ever done to grow the Dem majority to 56 seats?” a Democratic Senate aide told The Washington Sun about Sanders and Slotkin.

Van Hollen, a favorite among progressives who openly admits he’s also considering running for president, said there’s “a growing view” that the leadership election should not be a coronation. But he isn’t openly campaigning for the job. Pressed on whether he and Schumer had discussed the leadership race, Van Hollen said the two had been playing “phone tag” but that he would be pushing Schumer to advance a “bold agenda.”

He also touted his own early endorsement of Michigan’s Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and took a sharp jab at Schumer for interfering in Democratic primaries.

“We have two members in that room, newly elected senators, who would not be there if Schumer and the DSCC had had their way,” Van Hollen said. “And you know, Schumer and the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates.”

Van Hollen did not specify which senators-elect he was referring to. But Schumer backed moderates who lost their Senate primaries this year in Michigan and Maine.

A Democratic operative familiar with Senate races this cycle called Van Hollen’s statement “laughable,” noting that the main super PAC aligned with Schumer spent $67 million in support of El-Sayed after he defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, Schumer’s original pick, in the bitter Michigan Democratic primary.

“There are six senators who will be in the room because Schumer got them in or helped early,” the operative said.

A spokesperson for the DSCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
entries.author: Chase Pellegrini de Paur, Hunter Riggall, Igor Bobic

entries.title: House Democrats Blame Traffic for Missing Key Hegseth Impeachment Vote
entries.summary: “People should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote," said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove of her absent colleagues.
entries.content:
Eleven House Democrats missed a crucial vote Tuesday that could have kept an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth alive, drawing criticism from colleagues as several lawmakers blamed traffic delays for their absence.

The House voted 211-204 to send eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively blocking an immediate vote on impeachment.

The 11 missing Democrats had enough votes to defeat the motion, which would have failed 215-211 had they all voted against it, keeping the impeachment effort alive.

"We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote," Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-California) told reporters. "There is no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues."

"Shame on folks who are not here," she said. "Because these people lost. They lost, and they still found a way to show up to table this bill. Shameful."

A senior Democratic aide disputed that the votes of members blocked by traffic from returning to the Capitol would have changed the outcome, arguing that Republicans had only two members unavailable and closed the vote even though they knew more members were en route. 

The Washington Sun contacted the offices of the absent Democrats seeking explanations for their missed votes.

Three of the absent lawmakers, Reps. Steven Horsford (D-Nevada), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois) and Melanie Stansbury (D-New Mexico), blamed a traffic incident and a police-escorted bus that stalled intersections for preventing them from reaching the House floor in time.

"While en route to the floor to oppose that motion, a traffic incident and a police-escorted bus caused a delay that resulted in the vote closing before I, along with other Members, could reach the chamber," Horsford said in a statement to The Sun.

Jackson posted an identical statement on X. Stansbury's office said she reached the chamber just as the vote ended.

All three said they subsequently entered their opposition to the motion in the Congressional Record. Those statements did not change the official vote tally.

The office of Rep. Marilyn Strickland (D-Washington) also blamed a motorcade for her absence.

"The Congresswoman was stuck behind a motorcade and missed the vote by 1 minute. She would have voted against the motion to refer," her chief of staff, Andrew Noh, told The Sun.

Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-California) was in San Francisco attending a Veterans Day celebration, where she was being honored for her advocacy on behalf of veterans.

"Speaker Emerita Pelosi returned to San Francisco to join and honor local veterans at Swords to Plowshares’ 30th Annual Veterans Day Celebration tonight, an important and longstanding district tradition she regularly attends and will mark for the last time as a Member of Congress by receiving the Lifetime Advocate for Veterans Award," Pelosi spokesperson Ian Krager told The Sun.

"She supports impeaching Secretary Hegseth and would have voted ‘No’ on the motion to refer," Krager added.

Rep. Lou Correa (D-California) was also in his home state, where he said he was preparing to undergo a medical procedure and had been advised by his doctor to avoid traveling until he was medically cleared.

He did not say how he would have voted on the impeachment motion.

Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-Virginia) said the absent Democrats had been attending an event and failed to return in time.

"Should have never happened, but that's the way it played out," Vindman said.

The other absent Democrats were Reps. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan), Julia Brownley (D-California), Laura Gillen (D-New York), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colorado) and Frederica Wilson (D-Florida).

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Tuesday that he would discuss another impeachment effort against Hegseth with his members in the next Congress, when Democrats are set to take control of both the House and Senate.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) introduced the articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of violating congressional war powers, conducting unlawful military operations and abusing his authority at the Pentagon. Massie lost his reelection effort in a Republican primary to Trump-backed candidate Ed Gallrein.

entries.title: Capitals Beat Senators in Overtime, 3-2
entries.summary: Cole Hutson’s goal 74 seconds into overtime, set up by Alex Ovechkin, gave Washington to a 3-2 win.
entries.content:
OTTAWA, Ontario (AP) — Cole Hutson’s goal 74 seconds into overtime, set up by Alex Ovechkin, gave the Washington Capitals to a 3-2 win over the Ottawa Senators on Tuesday night.

The Capitals overcame a horrid second period in which they allowed two goals and trailed 2-1.

Matt Roy and Pierre-Luc Dubois also scored for the Capitals (10-6-0). Logan Thompson made 23 saves.

Ridly Greig and Hayden Hodgson scored for the Senators (11-6-2). Samuel Ersson stopped 14 shots.

Outshot 17-2 in the second period, Washington went more than 20 minutes before registering its next shot in the third period.

The Capitals showed life on the power play and maintained control after it expired and capitalized with Hutson finding Dubois at the side of the net for a wide-open shot to tie it at 2 at 12:31 of the third.

Ersson made a big save on Jack St. Ivany with four minutes remaining to keep the game tied.

With 2:57 remaining Jakob Chychrun leveled a huge hit on Nick Cousins, but no penalty was called. Cousins needed help getting off the ice.

Down 1-0 after the first, the Senators scored twice to lead 2-1 after 40 minutes.

Thomas Chabot set up both goals for the Senators.

On the first, Chabot kept the puck in at the blue line and fed Michael Amadio, who quickly passed it back. Chabot then found Greig in the slot, where he beat Thompson off his backhand.

Ottawa took the lead late in the period when Chabot took a pass from Stephen Halliday and put the puck through Chychrun’s legs to Hodgson for his first of the season.

The Capitals opened the scoring just 35 seconds into the game when Roy took a pass from Chychrun and fired a slap shot past Ersson for his first of the season.

Ryan Leonard played his 100th NHL game Tuesday. He has 26 goals and joins Alex Ovechkin (64), Alexander Semin (39), Dmitri Khristich (38) and Peter Bondra (29) as one of only five Capitals since 1990 to score 25 or more goals in their first 100 games.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: How Do You Host a Soccer Match and a Football Game on the Same Day?
entries.summary: D.C. United says it is “excited for the challenge” of Audi Field hosting the Spirit’s playoff game at noon and the Secretaries’ Cup at night.
entries.content:
After the Spirit plays its NWSL semifinal match Saturday at noon in Audi Field, the stadium will switch the playing surface from pro soccer to college football, load in new vendors, swap out team signage around the building and prepare for the service academy rivalry known as the Secretaries’ Cup — all in just a few hours.

“The Spirit earned the right to play a playoff match in front of their home crowd, and the cadets earned the right to play the Secretaries’ Cup on the stage that was promised to them,” Danita Johnson, president of business operations for D.C. United and Audi Field, told The Washington Sun. “We weren’t willing to choose between them, so we found a way to do both.”

Some last-minute dealmaking over the weekend allowed the Spirit to keep its semifinal game at Audi. That had been in doubt as the NWSL semifinal bracket solidified: Audi was booked months ago for the NCAA Division III Secretaries’ Cup, played annually between the U.S. Coast Guard Academy and U.S. Merchant Marine Academy, at 1 p.m. That would have made it impossible for the Spirit to host that day at 12 p.m.

Audi Field scheduling and operations are managed by D.C. United. (The Spirit are a full-time tenant of the stadium.) A scheduling conflict looked inevitable.

The NWSL did not want to push the Spirit game to a different time because of broadcast considerations and did not want to push the game to another day because of how it would affect the other side of the semifinal bracket. (No. 1 seed Gotham FC, which has seen its own stadium drama this week, plays on Sunday, with the additional day of rest a perk of being the highest seed.) The Secretaries’ Cup had been scheduled for months and had been in conversations with D.C. United leadership about hosting the game for nearly a year.

Spirit leadership prepared to host in another venue and secured Northwest Stadium, home of the Commanders, in Landover, Md. But the club knew that would not be ideal: It did not want to stage a do-or-die match in an unfamiliar stadium that was not built for soccer.

D.C. United decided the best course of action was hosting both events on the same day, with the Spirit at noon, and the Secretaries’ Cup in the evening.

“We understood the importance of Audi Field to the Spirit, as we always have, but we also have our commitment to the Secretaries’ Cup,” Johnson said. “It was trying to figure out: Is there a way that we could do something special? And that's what is coming to life currently.”

As of late Tuesday night, D.C. United was still working alongside the service academies to finalize a kickoff time for the Secretaries’ Cup.

Changing the field from soccer to football will involve painting yard lines and installing goalposts. It will be the venue’s first time attempting this kind of same-day turnover.

“It’s something new for us here at Audi Field, but we've seen it done in other venues, and we're excited for the challenge,” Johnson said.

The Spirit found a sponsor to underwrite a portion of the cost associated with shifting the schedule like this. (That portion was “in the low six figures,” according to a person with knowledge of the deal.) D.C. United is paying roughly $500,000.

“This was never about financial gain for Audi Field or our ownership group,” Johnson said. “It’s an additional cost to our organization, and we're prepared to take that on, being good partners to both.”

The Secretaries’ Cup has been played annually for nearly 50 years and traditionally alternated between the home fields of the two academies. Last year, it was played in Boston at Fenway Park, and Audi Field was publicly announced as the site of the 2026 game back in August.

The game has a slew of additional programming, including a ticketed fan fest, and could not be bumped to another day: This is the last weekend of the Division III football regular season and the selection show for the 40-team playoff bracket is held on Sunday.

“We’ve made a commitment to them well in advance, and I think honoring that commitment has remained a priority for us throughout this process,” Johnson said of the Secretaries’ Cup. “So we've been having extensive conversations with our organizers to work through the complexities of hosting two major events in the same day.”

entries.title: Biden’s Memoir Reveals What Trump Told Him Following Bitter 2020 Election
entries.summary: At the time of transition, Biden was said to have been surprised by how gracious he thought Trump's letter was.
entries.content:
By Meg Kinnard

President Donald Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed “will be true to yourself and the American people.”

That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn’t let anyone read it, describing it later that day as “very generous” but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.

Inclusion of the letter in Biden’s “Promise Me, America,” his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump's trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed “To ‘46,’” denoting Biden's place as the 46th U.S. president.

“Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats,” Trump wrote. “Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.”

At the time of transition, Biden was said to have been surprised by how gracious he thought the letter was, given the animosity between the political rivals. Trump had opted out of other presidential traditions, like attending Biden’s inauguration, or hosting the incoming president and first lady for tea at the White House.

Trump has said he thought it was up to Biden to share the letter, calling it “a nice note” during a September 2023 interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” adding, “I took a lot of time in thinking about it.”

Elsewhere in the memoir, the first excerpt of which was published Monday by the Atlantic, Biden wrote of the deep damage Trump has inflicted, with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”

Lamenting Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, Biden wrote of Trump’s “dismissive and destructive nature,” describing his predecessor and successor as someone “who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”

But Biden's harshest characterization so far was focused on Trump's role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, as Congress met to certify the 2020 election, which Biden had won. Writing that Trump “led an insurrection,” Biden said Trump's ”goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office."

“What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten,” Biden wrote. "It should follow him to his grave.”

Asked for comment on both the letter and Biden's memoir, White House communications director Steven Cheung called the former president “a disgrace" who “should have heeded the President’s wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies.”
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: White House to Oversight Democrats: We’ll Investigate You Right Back
entries.summary: The Trump administration said it’s ready to open criminal probes into Democrats for issuing subpoenas and using other investigative tools.
entries.content:
The White House said on Wednesday that it’s preparing to probe Democrats in connection with their efforts to conduct oversight of the executive branch, claiming that subpoenas and other investigative tools could “cross the line into blatant criminality.”

In a letter to incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-California), White House Counsel Will Scharf cautioned that Democrats cannot investigate Trump administration officials “for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators.”

Congressional members have also recently made public statements inferring they’ll issue subpoenas to “harass, threaten and deter dedicated members of the Administration from further service,” the letter, obtained by The Washington Sun, says.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

As evidence of Garcia’s ill intentions as Oversight chair, Scharf cited recent public statements made by the California Democrat instructing Trump administration officials to “lawyer up” and a recent interview in which he admitted to being at least partially motivated by spite.

“Maybe it’s because I’m gay, but pettiness is a thing,” Garcia said during an appearance at Crooked Con in Washington, D.C., last week.

The letter, first reported by Punchbowl News, is a sharp rebuke from the Trump administration, indicating it does not plan to cooperate with Democratic-led investigations and setting up two years of legal battles as Democrats pledge to probe the president and those around him for alleged corruption and mishandling of executive authority.

In a written statement responding to the letter, Garcia said, “It appears Donald Trump has something to hide.”

“The Trump administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress,” the statement continued. “We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the president’s lawyers.”

Rep. Stephen Lynch, another Democratic member of the Oversight Committee, also had a message for administration officials looking to open counter investigations against members of the panel: “Come at me, bro.”

Riding high off a historic midterm victory that saw Democrats flip a number of Republican districts en route to reclaiming the House and Senate, lawmakers immediately vowed to investigate what they characterized as the excesses of the Trump administration.

Rep.-elect Analilia Mejia (D-New Jersey) wrote on X: “We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads.”

And Texas Rep.-elect Katy Padilla Stout wrote: “Lawyer up, clear your schedules, & put some makeup on for the cameras.”

Scharf, however, said issuing subpoenas with the intention of depriving Trump officials of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant counter investigations.

“Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary,” he wrote.

Scharf began serving as White House counsel this year. He was previously an assistant to the president and a staff secretary. Prior to joining the White House, he ran for Missouri attorney general and was an assistant U.S. attorney at the Justice Department.

Democrats have a long list of investigations they’re likely to pursue in the new Congress, including accusations of corruption by President Donald Trump and his family members, alleged abuse and misconduct by immigration officials, and the potential misuse of executive power.

In an August letter to donors, Garcia said as chairman of the House Oversight Committee, he’ll compel testimony from the president’s family and advisers.

“If Democrats win back the House, I’ll become Chairman — and I’ll have subpoena power,” he wrote. “The power to subpoena Trump’s family, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Todd Blanche, and everyone involved in the Epstein files.”
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: D.C. Jail Inmates Were Among the First to See PBS’s New Criminal Justice Doc
entries.summary: “You can’t really understand America without knowing this story,” filmmaker Lynn Novick told the audience of pretrial detainees.
entries.content:
Javonte Robinson said he didn’t know much about the history of the U.S. criminal justice system before he found himself a part of it: confined in the D.C. jail awaiting trial, with a lot of time to reflect.

Now, he knows a whole lot more after watching an excerpt of a new, sweeping PBS documentary about crime and punishment in America. On Tuesday, Robinson and a group of several dozen detainees at the D.C. jail were among the first in the country to see a portion of the eight-hour film. Like many in the room, he left with an understanding that while the country’s justice system has evolved over the centuries, many of its deepest flaws persist.

“It was a lot of things that was eye-opening to me … when the first prisons first started, it was for people to get locked up and repent. Now it's for people to come get locked up and ‘rehabilitate,’” he said. But, he added, “it's basically the same; it's no rehabilitation because the recidivism rate is outrageous.”

The Tuesday screening, a 45-minute excerpt from the project, was the seventh showing of the documentary behind bars. It arrived as the D.C. jail is facing multiple class-action lawsuits over issues ranging from poor medical care to mice in food, and weeks after an inmate died in a stabbing. Lynn Novick, the director of the film, attended and took questions from viewers. What resulted was a robust discussion about the history of the criminal justice system, exactly the kind of dialogue Novick said she hoped the film would produce.

“You can’t really understand America without knowing this story, but I think most people don’t know the history,” she said, after one inmate asked her why she made the film. “Some of these are really hard questions, and I think we're so polarized and divided, we have not been able to have hard conversations and really dig deep into how to get to a better place. And I actually think that making this film the way we made it can help with that.”

The film excerpt took viewers from the era of public executions before the Revolutionary War to the 20th-century war on drugs and the present day. Along the way, it featured the perspectives of people who had been touched by the criminal justice system, from incarcerated people to crime victims to people who have worked in jails and prisons.

One inmate was particularly struck by the account of a former corrections officer who said that he took the job in part because he couldn’t achieve other career goals. During the Q&A after the film, he said the officer’s story gave him the idea that working in jails and prison was for many an “occupation by default.”

Reginald Dwayne Betts, a formerly incarcerated poet and advocate who was featured in the film, interrupted to push back.

“I wouldn’t think it was appropriate if anybody on this panel started making generalizations about who you guys are,” he said, urging the man to keep in mind that corrections officers are motivated to do the job for a variety of reasons.

A pair of D.C. corrections officers sat in the back of the screening, silent.

“I think the reason why we put that in the film is to have this conversation,” said Novick, “and to be able to have the potential that we can see everybody as human beings … people who are confined here and people who work here are subject to difficult conditions.”

Robinson was struck by how far back in history the film went, to the Code of Hammurabi and the concepts of crime and punishment in religion. He said he was shocked to learn the true story of American folk hero John Henry — who, according to the documentary, was likely a teenage convict, locked up on a petty theft charge, leased to work on a railroad and then died because of poor working conditions. “I didn’t know that,” Robinson said. He wondered if his new knowledge could help him navigate the justice system — and “maybe I can help somebody else through my experience,” he said.

The film, geared toward a general audience and designed in many ways to teach people with no personal experience of incarceration, hit close to home in the room, a small chapel behind the jail’s thick gray walls.

Watching it was “powerful and painful,” reflected one inmate, who asked to be referred to by his first name, Abraham. An Ethiopian immigrant, he got emotional as he described the moment he walked into the D.C. jail — and how it put the racial disparities the film highlighted into instant relief.

“I still cannot forget,” he said, “how I felt seeing the amount of Black people.”
entries.author: Jenny Gathright

entries.title: Republicans Struggle to Find One Last Win in Congress
entries.summary: “None of the Venn diagrams work to get to 51, in my judgment, right now,” said Sen. Thom Tillis about moving a reconciliation bill.
entries.content:
Fresh off of the midterm elections that have Republicans licking their wounds from a massive blowout flipping control of both chambers, lawmakers are attempting to use the lame-duck session to revive hopes of getting a third budget reconciliation bill approved.

However, they are finding the road and the timetable treacherous. Senate Majority Leader John Thune indicated that he still is not sure whether the party has the votes to advance a single-party measure of any kind, despite hopes that they could be unlocked postelection.

“That’s always the drill with reconciliation: What’s possible? What can you get 50 votes for, and that’s tough because everybody’s got different ideas,” said Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota. “Of course, now you had the election, so everybody’s talking about what else? And that’s where we’re at.”

Republican members discussed the options during a party luncheon last Wednesday, a day after Thune and the rest of the leadership team were reelected to their posts to serve in the minority next year.

The unrest inside the Republican conference over the midterm results prompted Thune to announce that members can expect to “stretch the calendar” in order to approve scores of judges and executive branch nominees before ceding control of the chamber in the new year.

The conference also adopted a resolution on Tuesday to serve as their guiding light for the next month and a half. On top of the nomination spree, it called for the conference “to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill” before Democrats take over.

Time is tight, though. Thune told reporters that members must make a decision by Thanksgiving, at the very latest. Hoeven, an appropriator, indicated that a call must come even earlier.

“We have to be moving,” Hoeven said. “We’re scheduling it out and having the conversation. … We got to get moving if we’re going to get it done.”

However, the lawmakers who were against a third bill preelection are showing few signs of changing their tune.

Sens. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, among others, remain skeptical of a budget resolution over concerns about the Iran war and going around appropriators to green-light defense funding, a likely cornerstone of a potential package.

“We need to be realistic about whether or not we can get the votes,” Tillis told reporters. “There's a lot of people that are for reconciliation. The problem is, it's for their version of reconciliation and there are probably four or five different versions out there, and none of the Venn diagrams work to get to 51, in my judgment, right now.”

The calendar is another complicating factor. Republicans have just over six weeks of control left and an ambitious to-do list, with little time for a time-consuming negotiation of whether a third reconciliation bill is something worth pursuing.

If they did move ahead, that interferes with their plan to confirm as many of Trump’s nominees as possible, as no other business could be considered while a reconciliation bill is on the floor. There remain two-dozen of judges who Republicans hope to confirm, on top of a wide swath of posts to fill throughout the administration.

“Nobody's throwing in the towel yet,” one Senate GOP aide said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. “But people are internalizing the list of things to do and simultaneously realizing that if you do one thing on the floor you're not doing another thing.”

There’s also vote constraints that will come into play. Sen.-elect Kevin Hern will be sworn in by the end of the month, depriving House Republicans of a vote. Thune met with incoming House Minority Leader Jim Jordan on Wednesday.

Senate Republicans will also see their majority dwindle next month when Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is sworn into office, giving them less wiggle room.

Members have also discussed the possibility of including a debt limit increase in order to take that off the table for Democrats to use as leverage next year, but Hoeven said that there is no “definitive plan” on that front.

Nevertheless, there remains an intense desire to approve something. Prior to the election, any bill would have centered on $350 billion that the Pentagon has requested, funding related to the SAVE America voting bill and aid for farmers and areas affected by natural disasters.

The postelection push has expanded that potential pot, even though members remain cognizant that if a bill were to move, they have limited bandwidth to do so.

“It’s no excuse that, well, it may be hard to get the votes. If your conclusion is that we shouldn’t try reconciliation because it might be hard to get the votes, then congratulations, you’re stupid,” said Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a leading proponent of passing a third measure.

“You can’t put 12 things into a four-thing box. We ought to be able to agree on money for defense, and we ought to be able to agree on at least one other policy,” he added.

Kennedy, name checked Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst’s anti-fraud bill as a possibility, saying the juice was worth the squeeze for one last big ticket item to conclude the Republican trifecta.

“I think we ought to surprise ourselves and do something intelligent and show the American people that we heard them,” he said. “You can talk yourself out of anything, and I concede this may fail. But why not try?”

Others believe that the party is not taking the message sent by voters to heart, especially on funding the Iran war.

“The number one issue that came out of the election and the exit polls, that the vice president admitted — was the war and the price of gasoline,” Paul told The Washington Sun. “For Republicans to immediately come back and, by sheer might with just Republicans, finance [the] Iran war, I think, seems to me like they didn't listen.”
entries.author: Al Weaver
